bib.title: Kimi-Dev: Agentless Training as Skill Prior for SWE-Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Kimi-Dev: Agentless Training as Skill Prior for SWE-Agents", Zonghan Yang* and Shengjie Wang* (equal contribution; joint leads Yang and Tianyu Liu), plus Moonshot AI, THU, PKU co-authors. arXiv:2509.23045v3 (cs.AI), dated 8 Dec 2025 (v1 would be Sep 2025). No venue printed, so treat as preprint.

COVERAGE: 68 of 68 pages read (extraction 173,987 chars). Body (pp.1-10) read in full. Appendices read in full for A (mid-training recipe), C (RL ablations), F (parallel scaling) and G (agent analysis, G.4 generalization). Prompt listings, long case-study traces (E, G.2, G.3) and the reference list were skimmed. Figures 5, 6, 7, 11 and 12 are charts, so only the text describing them was read, not the plotted values.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Agentless training (mid-train, SFT cold-start, RL) gives a better starting point for SWE-agent adaptation. The RL-stage prior reaches the Base prior's best score with far less agent SFT data.
 number: 2^23 vs 1.5x2^28 SWE-Agent SFT tokens (roughly 64x fewer, my arithmetic)
 setup: Qwen2.5-72B Base, MT, SFT and RL priors, each fine-tuned on nested subsets (100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000 of 5,016 SWE-smith Claude 3.7 trajectories). Baselines are zero-shot and one gradient step. SWE-bench Verified, pass@1 at temp 0, pass@2/3 at temp 1. Run count is not stated for Fig 5.
 quote: "To achieve the top pass@1 performance of the Base prior, the RL prior needs only 2^23 SWE-Agent SFT tokens, whereas the Base prior consumes 1.5×2^28 tokens."
 where: p.9
2. This is the ablation that matters for the SFT-vs-RL question. The SFT-only prior dips sharply at 200 trajectories. The authors suggest memorization, and say the RL prior generalizes better. This is an explanation, not a tested mechanism.
 number: none (the drop is shown only in Fig 5)
 setup: same sweep as claim 1. The SFT prior is Qwen2.5-72B after the Agentless long-CoT SFT. The RL prior is the same model after RL.
 quote: "The SFT prior exhibits a significant degradation with 200 SWE-Agent trajectories (2^24). A potential reason could be that the 200 trajectories collapse onto a single data mode, leading the SFT prior to overfit through memorization (Chu et al., 2025); the RL prior instead embeds stronger transferable skills and thus generalizes better."
 where: p.9
 Caveat in the same list: SFT beats RL at zero-shot, "as the RL prior might overfit to the Agentless input-output format". Otherwise SFT and RL are "mostly similar".
3. Headline: Kimi-Dev 72B reaches 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified in the Agentless workflow, the best among workflow methods. After SFT on 5k public trajectories it reaches 48.6% pass@1 in SWE-Agent, no agentic RL.
 number: 60.4% and 48.6%
 setup: 72B from Qwen2.5-72B-Base. Agentless uses 40 patches x 40 tests with self-play. SWE-Agent adaptation uses 5,016 SWE-smith trajectories from Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 64K training context, up to 128K tokens and 100 turns at inference.
 baselines: SWE-SWISS 32B 58.2, DeepSeek-R1-0528 671B 57.6, MiniMax-M1 56.0 (Agentless-like, Table 1). Claude 3.5 Sonnet 241022 scores 49.0 under SWE-Agent (Table 2).
 quote: "our finetuned model achieves a pass@1 score of 48.6% on SWE-bench Verified under the agentic framework setup, without additional test-time scaling."
 where: p.8 and Tables 1-2 (pp.5, 7)
 Table 2 shows it is far below the strongest agent systems: Qwen3-Coder 69.6, Kimi-K2-0905 69.2, Devstral-Small 53.6, gpt-oss-20b 60.7.
4. Test-time self-play (BugFixer patches scored by TestWriter tests) lifts the score from 48.0% to 60.4%, and beats majority vote.
 number: 48.0% to 60.4%
 setup: patch-test pairs grown from 1x1 to 40x40. Greedy first rollout, temp 1 for the other 39. SWE-bench Verified.
 quote: "the final performance improves from 48.0% to 60.4% as the number of patch-test pairs increases from 1×1 to 40×40"
 where: p.6
 Also: 3 patches x 3 tests already beats majority vote over 40 patches. Self-play stays below pass@N with ground-truth tests, so TestWriter is the bottleneck.
5. Reflection from long CoT transfers to longer agent horizons. After adaptation on all 5,016 trajectories, pass@3 under turn limits keeps improving past 70 turns for the RL prior. Diminishing returns come around 70 turns for SFT, 60 for MT and 50 for Base.
 number: Stage-3 cutoff resolves 484 (Base) vs 605 (RL) cases; reflection gain +94 (Base) vs +113 (RL)
 setup: counts over 3 runs (pass@3), SWE-bench Verified. Stages annotated by kimi-k2-0711-preview.
 quote: "ranging from 484 cases resolved by the Base prior to 605 cases by the RL prior"
 where: p.9
 The authors call the reflection analysis "coarse-grained".
6. End-to-end SWE-Agent RL comparison. Starting from one gradient step of agent SFT (2^21 tokens), the RL prior ends only slightly above the SFT prior. The MT prior collapses.
 number: pass@1 for the MT prior falls below 2% after 10 RL steps
 setup: 300 RL steps, batch 256, outcome reward only, no KL or entropy regularization. Problems with pass@8=0 are filtered (MT keeps 260 of 6,202; SFT and RL priors keep 2,062 of 6,202). Fig 7 pass@1 is averaged over 5 runs.
 quote: "the model with the RL prior demonstrates slightly higher scores of Pass@1, Pass@3, and Pass@5 over the model with the SFT prior."
 where: p.10
 The gap is described as "slightly", and no significance test is given.
7. Pass@10 of the adapted SWE-Agent (74.0%) exceeds pass@30 of the Agentless model (73.8%). The authors read this as higher potential for the agent framework.
 quote: "The pass@10 of our SWE-Agent adapted model is 74.0% and surpasses the pass@30 of our model under Agentless (73.8%)"
 where: p.8
8. Mid-training scale helps: 50B, 100B and ~150B tokens give a monotone improvement in BugFixer pass@1 (Fig 2, values not in the text). Mid-training data is about 150B tokens (~50B Agentless-form diffs, ~20B PR commit packs, ~20B synthetic data upsampled 4x).
 setup: Qwen2.5-72B-Base, then a 2,000-example SFT activation.
 quote: "Mid-training sufficiently enhances the knowledge in the model about practical bug fixes and unit tests"
 where: p.4-5
9. RL recipe (relevant to notes 06 and 07): REINFORCE-style, from Kimi k1.5, with the mean of rollouts as the baseline. Outcome reward only (0/1 from test execution), no format or process reward. Prompts with pass@16=0 are dropped, then 500 hard prompts are re-added every 100 steps. Positive-example reinforcement is added late in training.
 number: 1,200 initial prompts; 10 rollouts x 1,024 problems; 64k max context; sandbox "over 10,000 concurrent instances" (Kubernetes)
 quote: "Outcome-based reward only: We rely solely on the final execution outcome from the environment as the raw reward (0 or 1), without incorporating any format- or process-based signals."
 where: p.4
 Ablation: positive-example reinforcement gave better BugFixer RL (Fig 8, App C.2, numbers not in text). A 14B Qwen2.5-Instruct run showed the same RL scaling (Fig 9).
10. Out of distribution (SWE-bench-Live, 300 tasks; SWE-bench Multilingual, 300 tasks, 9 languages): the SFT and RL priors beat Base mainly when agent data is scarce. The gap closes as more trajectories are added.
 quote: "when more SWE-Smith trajectories are used for adaptation, the performances of the Base and the MT priors become closer to those of the SFT and the RL priors."
 where: p.67

LIMITS
- Only one model family (Qwen2.5-72B) is used for the prior comparison. 14B appears only for RL scaling.
- The memorization explanation for the SFT dip at 200 trajectories is a hypothesis. It rests on a single sweep point and cites Chu et al. 2025.
- The SFT vs RL prior gap is small in most settings and in end-to-end RL. SFT is better at zero-shot. No seeds, error bars or confidence intervals are described for the Fig 5 sweep. Fig 7 averages 5 runs.
- The prior is "RL on single-turn Agentless tasks". This is not RL on agent trajectories. The comparison is "mid-train + SFT" vs "mid-train + SFT + Agentless RL", so it is not a clean SFT-only vs RL-only comparison. The RL prior also gets more data and compute.
- TestWriter has false positives from weak test coverage (App E.2). Self-play stays below ground-truth pass@N.
- Reflection and BugFixer skill measures are coarse. The reflection measure also includes test-writing. The TestWriter prior was not isolated.
- Out-of-distribution gains vanish with enough agent data. The authors leave task-agnostic generalization to future work.
- The agent SFT data comes from Claude 3.7 Sonnet in synthetic SWE-smith environments, so proprietary imitation may contaminate "skill prior" effects. The authors partly mitigate this with the 2^21-token setting.
- The parallel-scaling result (App F, Fig 10) is "preliminary" and reported only as a figure.
- Python-centric training environments (SWE-Gym, SWE-bench-extra, R2E-Gym-Lite). Multilingual is evaluated only after adaptation.
- No claim about domains outside SWE.

BUILDS ON: Chu et al. 2025 ("SFT memorizes, RL generalizes", ICML 2025) for the memorization framing. Xia et al. 2024 (Agentless). Kimi k1.5 (Team et al. 2025) for the policy-gradient RL. REINFORCE (Williams 1992) and GRPO-style baselines (Shao et al. 2024). SWE-RL (Wei et al. 2025). SWE-smith (Yang et al. 2025b) for trajectories. SWE-Gym (Pan et al. 2024), SWE-bench-extra (Badertdinov et al. 2024), R2E-Gym (Jain et al. 2025). DeepSWE (Luo et al. 2025) for end-to-end agent RL. DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025) for cold-start data. Gudibande et al. 2024 (imitation limits). Finn et al. 2017 and Brown et al. 2020 for the few-shot-adaptation framing.

CODE: none worth keeping. The appendix prompt templates are verbatim, and the one reusable idea is the self-play selection score in Eq. 1 (p.5): S_i = sum_j FP(i,j)/sum_j F(j) + sum_j PP(i,j)/sum_j P(j).

FIGURES (captions from extraction; not rendered)
- Fig 5, p.8: the four priors (Base, MT, SFT, RL) vs SWE-Agent SFT tokens, pass@1/2/3. Best single visual for the SFT-vs-RL adaptation-efficiency claim, including the SFT dip at 2^24.
- Fig 6, p.9: turn-limit curves, plus BugFixer and reflection counts per prior.
- Fig 7, p.10: SFT prior vs RL prior after end-to-end RL, with pass@1 averaged over 5 runs.
- Fig 3, p.6: RL curves in which performance and response length rise together.
- Fig 4, p.6: self-play vs majority vote vs pass@N.
- Figs 11-12, p.68: out-of-distribution priors on SWE-bench-Live and Multilingual.

PROBLEMS: None blocking. Text extraction is clean. Some Fig 5-12 values exist only in charts, so they are not quoted. No embedded instructions found. Prompt listings in the appendix contain instruction-like text, but it is part of the paper's data and was ignored.

VERBATIM QUOTES FOR THE NOTE (2-3 with pages): p.9 SFT-dip memorization quote (claim 2). p.9 efficiency quote (claim 1). p.4 outcome-only reward quote (claim 9).
